candidate.answerReason: Placing a 60-meter side along the wall requires 132 meters of fence, giving 11 gaps and 12 posts. Placing a 36-meter side along the wall requires 156 meters of fence and 14 posts. Both orientations fit the 100-meter wall.

methods.label: Compare the two orientations and count gaps
methods.explanation:
Equal spacing suggests counting the \(12\)-meter gaps first. The three fenced sides form one continuous path, with a post at each end where it meets the wall.

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_8_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

A side against the wall can have length \(60\) meters or \(36\) meters. Both fit along the \(100\)-meter wall.

With a \(60\)-meter side against the wall, the fenced sides have total length
\[
36+60+36=132\text{ meters}.
\]
This gives \(132\div12=11\) gaps. Starting with the first post, each gap leads to one additional post, so there are \(11+1=12\) posts.

With a \(36\)-meter side against the wall, the fence length is
\[
60+36+60=156\text{ meters},
\]
requiring \(156\div12+1=14\) posts. In both arrangements, the side lengths are multiples of \(12\), so the spacing places posts at the corners, and each shared corner is counted just once along the continuous path.

These are the only two side lengths that can lie along the wall. Therefore the fewest posts required is \(\boxed{12}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The method uses rectangle side lengths, whole-number division, and the elementary relationship between gaps and posts on a path with both endpoints included.

candidate.annotationRationale: The central target is distinguishing the number of equally spaced gaps from the number of posts when both endpoints are included. Rectangle boundary-length reasoning supports comparing the two orientations. Opposite-side equality and division by a two-digit spacing are local prerequisites. No area optimization, algebraic inequality, or general extremal theorem is needed. These assignments do not establish student mastery.

review.mathematicalCheck: Both possible wall-side lengths fit the 100-meter wall. Using 60 meters leaves 132 meters of fence, giving 11 gaps and 12 posts; using 36 meters leaves 156 meters, giving 13 gaps and 14 posts. All side lengths are multiples of 12, so corner posts respect the spacing. The two orientations exhaust the possibilities and establish the minimum.
review.levelCheck: The arithmetic, rectangle properties, and endpoint counting are appropriate for AMC 8.
review.methodDistinctness: One method comparing both orientations completely resolves the minimum.
review.annotationCheck: The assessed planting-problem node captures the decisive gaps-plus-one relationship. Rectangle boundary-length reasoning, opposite-side equality, and division with a two-digit divisor justify the support and prerequisite assignments.
